title: La Paz Batchoy
description: Fresh miki noodles in a garlicky pork-bone broth loaded with pork strips and sliced liver, finished with crushed chicharon and toasted garlic — Iloilo's answer to ramen, sold in every La Paz market stall.

ingredients.item: pork belly or shoulder, thinly sliced

ingredients.note: or omit and add extra pork belly for a milder bowl
homemade or use good-quality stock cubes dissolved in water
or substitute fresh egg noodles
fry the reserved minced garlic in oil until golden

steps: Bring the bone broth to a boil in a large pot, then lower to a simmer and add the onion, half the garlic and the shrimp paste; simmer 15 minutes to build flavour.
Season the broth with onion powder, sugar and salt to taste, then keep it at a gentle simmer.
Heat the oil in a small pan and fry the remaining garlic over low heat until golden and crisp; scoop out the garlic bits and reserve the garlic oil separately.
Slip the sliced pork into the simmering broth and poach 4-5 minutes until just cooked through; lift out with a slotted spoon and set aside.
Add the sliced liver to the same broth and poach 1-2 minutes until it just loses its pink colour, then lift out.
Blanch the fresh miki noodles in the broth 1-2 minutes until tender, then divide the noodles among deep bowls.
Top each bowl of noodles with the poached pork and liver, then ladle the hot broth over everything.
Finish each bowl with crushed chicharon, toasted garlic bits, a drizzle of garlic oil and chopped green onions; serve immediately while the chicharon is still crunchy.
tips: Add the chicharon only at the table, never in advance — it turns soggy within minutes of hitting hot broth.
Poaching the liver separately and briefly keeps it tender instead of turning it grainy and bitter.
A splash of the garlic-infused frying oil stirred into the broth just before serving is what gives La Paz-style batchoy its signature aroma.
nutritionNote: A rich, protein-heavy bowl between the pork, liver and broth; serve smaller portions of chicharon topping and add a side of blanched vegetables to round out the meal, since this is a heavier main than an everyday soup.

title: Pancit Molo
description: Pork-and-shrimp dumplings simmered in a light garlicky chicken broth, despite the name a soup rather than a stir-fried noodle — the Molo district of Iloilo's cold-weather comfort food.

ingredients.note: to taste
rotisserie or leftover boiled chicken works well

ingredients.item: toasted garlic bits and chopped green onions

steps: Combine the ground pork, shrimp, garlic, green onions, soy sauce, salt and pepper in a bowl and mix well to make the filling.
Lay out a wonton wrapper, spoon about a teaspoon of filling in the centre, moisten the edges with water and fold into a small dumpling, pressing to seal; repeat with the remaining wrappers.
Heat the oil in a deep pot over medium heat and sauté the onion and garlic until softened and fragrant.
Add the shredded chicken and stir 1-2 minutes to warm through.
Pour in the chicken broth and fish sauce, bring to a boil, then lower to a simmer.
Drop the dumplings into the simmering broth in batches so they don't stick together, and cook 5-6 minutes until they float and the filling is cooked through.
Taste the broth and adjust salt or fish sauce as needed.
Ladle the soup and dumplings into bowls and garnish with toasted garlic bits and green onions before serving.
tips: Make a double batch of dumplings and freeze half uncooked on a tray before bagging — they can go straight from freezer to simmering broth.
Don't overfill the wrappers; a slightly smaller dumpling holds together better and cooks more evenly in the broth.
Shredded rotisserie chicken is a real time-saver here and gives the broth extra body from the start.
nutritionNote: A well-rounded soup with protein from pork, shrimp and chicken already built in; serve as a light meal with steamed rice on the side rather than as a starter, since the dumplings make it fairly filling.

title: Goto
description: Rice porridge simmered with tender ox tripe into a thick, savoury congee, topped with boiled egg, scallions and chicharon — a rib-sticking breakfast bowl sold from carts before sunrise.

ingredients.item: ox tripe, cleaned and cut into bite-sized strips
ingredients.note: ask the butcher to pre-clean it; rinse again at home before cooking
gives the porridge its golden colour
for the dipping side sauce

steps: Place the ox tripe in a large pot, cover generously with water, and boil 1.5-2 hours, topping up water as needed, until fork-tender; drain and set aside, reserving 1.5 litres of the cooking liquid as stock.
Rinse the rice and set aside.
Heat the oil in a deep pot and sauté the onion, ginger and half the garlic until softened and fragrant.
Add the cooked tripe and turmeric powder, stirring 1-2 minutes to coat.
Add the rice and the reserved tripe stock (topping up with plain water if short), bring to a boil, then lower the heat to a gentle simmer.
Cook uncovered 30-40 minutes, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking, until the rice breaks down into a thick porridge.
Stir in the fish sauce and adjust the consistency with a splash more water if it becomes too thick.

In a small pan, fry the remaining garlic in a little oil until golden; ladle the goto into bowls and top with a halved boiled egg, toasted garlic, chicharon and green onions, serving with calamansi and soy sauce on the side.
tips: Simmering the tripe low and slow in plenty of water, rather than rushing it, is what makes it tender instead of chewy.
The porridge thickens a lot as it sits — loosen leftovers with extra broth or water when reheating.
Toast the garlic separately from the aromatics so it stays crisp as a topping instead of going soft in the porridge.
nutritionNote: A filling breakfast porridge that's high in protein from the tripe and egg but low in fibre; add a side of sliced tomato or fruit and go easy on the chicharon topping to keep the meal balanced.

title: Kwek-Kwek
description: Hard-boiled quail eggs dipped in a bright orange annatto batter and deep-fried until crisp, served on sticks with a sweet-tangy dip — the orange-egg street snack found outside every school gate.

ingredients.note: for dredging
gives the classic orange colour
with a pinch of salt, garlic and chili to taste

steps: Dredge each peeled quail egg lightly in cornstarch, shaking off the excess, and set aside.
In a mixing bowl, whisk the flour, batter cornstarch, annatto powder, water, salt and pepper into a smooth, thick batter roughly the consistency of pancake batter.
Heat the oil in a wok or deep pan to 350°F (180°C).
Dip each dredged egg into the batter, coating it fully, then carefully lower it into the hot oil.
Fry in batches, without crowding the pan, 2-3 minutes until the coating is crisp and deep orange.
Lift out with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towels.
Skewer 3-4 eggs onto bamboo sticks if serving street-food style.
Serve hot with the spiced vinegar dip or a sweet chili sauce on the side.
tips: Dredging the eggs in cornstarch before battering helps the batter cling instead of sliding off in the oil.
Keep the oil at a steady medium-hot temperature — too hot and the coating browns before the batter sets; too cool and it turns greasy.
Pre-boiled and peeled quail eggs are sold in Filipino grocers and are worth buying to save time.
kidNote: Skip the chili in the dipping vinegar for the kids' portion and offer a plain sweet-chili or banana ketchup dip instead; quail eggs are small, so remind younger kids to chew slowly.
nutritionNote: A fried, cornstarch-heavy snack best treated as an occasional treat rather than a meal; pair with fresh fruit afterward and keep portions to a few pieces per serving.

title: Turon
description: Ripe saba bananas and a sliver of jackfruit rolled in a spring roll wrapper and fried until the sugar coating caramelizes into a shattering shell — the everyday afternoon merienda sold by the roadside in every province.

ingredients.note: or use ripe plantains if saba is unavailable

ingredients.item: ripe jackfruit, sliced into thin strips
ingredients.note: canned or fresh; optional but traditional

steps: Roll each banana half in the granulated sugar until well coated on all sides.
Lay a lumpia wrapper on a clean surface with one corner pointing toward you, place a sugared banana half near the bottom corner and top with a strip of jackfruit.
Fold the bottom corner over the filling, fold in the sides, then roll up tightly, sealing the top corner with a dab of water.
Repeat with the remaining bananas and wrappers.
Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium heat and sprinkle in a spoonful of the remaining sugar; let it start to melt before adding the turon.
Fry the turon in batches, turning occasionally, 4-5 minutes until the wrapper is golden brown and the sugar coating has caramelized.
Lift out with tongs onto a wire rack or lightly oiled plate to cool slightly — the caramel is very hot.
Serve warm on its own or with a scoop of vanilla ice cream.
tips: Letting a little sugar caramelize directly in the frying oil, not just on the banana, is what gives turon its shattering shell.
Cool the fried turon on a rack rather than stacking them, or the caramel will glue the pieces together.
Turon is best eaten fresh; the wrapper turns soggy if refrigerated, so freeze uncooked rolls instead if making ahead.
nutritionNote: A sugary, deep-fried treat best kept to a once-in-a-while merienda rather than a daily one; one piece alongside fresh fruit is plenty for a child's snack.

title: Banana Cue
description: Whole saba bananas deep-fried and rolled in melting brown sugar until they're glazed and sticky, then skewered on bamboo sticks — a three-ingredient snack sold from carts every late afternoon.

ingredients.note: ripe but firm, with yellow skin and a few black spots
helps the sugar melt into an even syrup rather than clumping
optional, stirred into the sugar to cut the sweetness slightly

steps: Heat the oil in a wok or deep pan over medium heat to about 350°F (180°C).
Add the peeled bananas in batches, without crowding the pan, and fry 4-5 minutes, turning occasionally, until golden and tender.
Sprinkle in half the brown sugar with a splash of the water and a pinch of salt, and keep tossing the bananas gently so they get evenly coated as the sugar melts and caramelizes.
Once the sugar turns a light amber and clings to the bananas, lift them out quickly with tongs before it burns.
Repeat with the remaining bananas and sugar in the next batch.
While still hot, skewer two bananas onto each bamboo stick.
Let the caramel set for a minute or two before serving warm.
tips: Work quickly once the sugar starts to caramelize — it goes from glossy to burnt in under a minute.
Firmer, not overly ripe, saba bananas hold their shape better in the hot oil than very soft ones.
Skewer the bananas immediately after frying, while the caramel is still pliable enough to set around the stick.
nutritionNote: A simple caramelized-fruit snack that's still high in added sugar and frying oil; treat it as an occasional after-school treat rather than a daily merienda, and pair with a glass of milk instead of a sweet drink.

title: Maruya
description: Mashed saba bananas folded into a simple sweet batter and pan-fried into golden fritters, rolled warm in sugar — a softer, batter-based cousin of banana cue that turns up at breakfast tables and merienda trays alike.
steps: In a large bowl, combine the flour, baking powder, salt and half the sugar; mix well.
Gradually fold in the mashed bananas.
Add the beaten egg, vanilla extract and milk, and mix until you have a thick, scoopable batter.
Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium heat.
Scoop about 1/3 cup of batter per fritter into the hot oil, flattening it slightly with the back of the spoon.
Fry 2-3 minutes per side until both sides turn golden brown.
Drain briefly on paper towels, then sprinkle the remaining sugar over both sides while still warm.
Serve warm on their own or with a drizzle of condensed milk.
tips: Very ripe, sweet bananas mean you can dial back the added sugar in the batter itself.
Fry over medium, not high, heat so the fritters cook through before the outside over-browns.
Sugar the fritters while they're still warm — it won't stick once they've cooled and the surface dries.
nutritionNote: A fried, sugared breakfast treat that's fine alongside a protein like eggs or milk to balance the meal; keep it as a once-or-twice-a-week breakfast rather than an everyday one given the oil and sugar.

title: Taho
description: Warm silken tofu layered with chewy sago pearls and a brown sugar syrup, scooped into cups the way tahô vendors have sold it from balanced buckets at dawn for generations.

ingredients.note: steamed or microwaved just until heated through

steps: Cook the sago pearls in the 3 cups of water at a low boil, stirring occasionally, 15-20 minutes until translucent all the way through.
Drain the cooked sago, rinse briefly with warm water to stop it from clumping, and set aside.
Combine the brown sugar, 1 cup water and vanilla in a small saucepan and bring to a boil, stirring until the sugar dissolves.
Lower the heat and simmer the syrup 2-4 minutes until it thickens slightly into a syrup that coats a spoon; set aside to cool a little.
Steam the silken tofu for about 8 minutes, or microwave in a covered dish for about 1 minute, until warmed through.
Using a wide, shallow spoon, scoop thin layers of the warm tofu into serving cups or glasses.
Top each cup with a spoonful of cooked sago and a generous drizzle of the brown sugar syrup.
Serve immediately while the tofu is still warm.
tips: Scooping the tofu with a flat, wide spoon rather than cubing it gives the silky, ribbon-like texture vendors are known for.
Warm, not hot, syrup blends better into the tofu without breaking it apart.
Leftover sago and syrup keep well chilled for a few days — just reheat the tofu fresh each time.
nutritionNote: A light, protein-rich breakfast from the soy tofu, though the syrup and sago add a fair amount of sugar; go easy on the syrup drizzle for younger kids and pair with a piece of fruit.

title: Shrimp and Sweet Potato Fritters
description: Shredded sweet potato and small whole shrimp bound in a thin batter and fried into crisp, lacy patties, served with spiced vinegar for dipping — a favourite merienda that also works as a side dish with rice.

ingredients.item: sweet potato, peeled and coarsely grated

ingredients.note: or peeled shrimp for younger kids who dislike shells
for colour; optional

ingredients.item: cane vinegar with garlic and chili
ingredients.note: to taste

steps: In a large bowl, whisk the flour, cornstarch, egg, water, annatto powder, salt and pepper into a thin, pourable batter.
Fold in the grated sweet potato until evenly coated.
Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium heat.

Using a small saucer or the back of a ladle, spread a thin layer of the sweet potato mixture and press 2-3 shrimp on top before sliding it into the hot oil, or simply drop spoonfuls of the mixture with shrimp pressed on top directly into the oil.
Fry 3-4 minutes per side, pressing gently to flatten, until the fritter is golden brown, crisp and lacy at the edges.
Drain on paper towels.
Repeat with the remaining mixture, keeping the oil at a steady medium heat.
Serve hot with the spiced vinegar dip.
tips: A thinner batter gives the classic lacy, crisp edge — don't thicken it with extra flour if it looks loose.
Frying in a single thin layer rather than a thick patty is what makes ukoy crunchy all the way through.
Peeled shrimp work fine and make the fritters easier for younger kids to eat without picking around shells.
nutritionNote: A fried snack that still carries real vegetable and protein value from the sweet potato and shrimp; good as an occasional side with rice and a simple soup rather than a daily fried treat.

title: Sweet Rice Balls in Coconut Milk
description: Chewy glutinous rice balls, ripe jackfruit and sago pearls simmered in sweetened coconut cream until warm and fragrant — a home-style merienda soup eaten by the bowlful on rainy afternoons.

ingredients.note: add gradually until the dough is soft and pliable
canned or fresh

ingredients.item: ripe saba bananas, sliced into rounds
ingredients.note: traditional addition alongside the jackfruit

steps: Combine the glutinous rice flour with water a little at a time, kneading until you have a soft, non-sticky dough.
Pinch off small pieces and roll into marble-sized balls (bilo-bilo); set aside on a lightly floured plate.
Bring the 2 cups of water to a boil in a wide pot, then stir in the coconut cream and return to a gentle boil.
Gradually stir in the sugar until dissolved.
Add the jackfruit and sliced banana, cover and simmer over low heat 10-12 minutes until the banana softens slightly.
Drop in the bilo-bilo rice balls and simmer, stirring gently every few minutes so they don't stick to the bottom, 12-15 minutes until they float and turn firm but chewy.
Stir in the pre-cooked sago pearls and simmer 3-5 minutes more to heat through.
Ladle into bowls and serve warm.
tips: Roll the rice balls just before cooking — the dough dries and cracks if it sits too long uncovered.
Keep the heat low once the coconut cream goes in; a hard boil can cause it to separate and turn oily.
Stir gently and only occasionally once the rice balls are in, or they can break apart into the soup.
nutritionNote: Rich in saturated fat from the coconut cream despite being a fruit-and-rice-based dessert; serve smaller bowls as an afternoon snack rather than a dessert on top of a full meal, especially alongside other coconut-milk dishes that week.
